items.name: Readability
items.evidence: There are no comments, either on the `#/*` … `#*/` / `r"""` trick or on the base-1e9 bignum loop. Business-logic variables are single letters (`a`, `b`, `n`) plus `cap`, `idx`, `len`. Formatting is clean and consistent.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The C side is one monolithic `main` of about 45 lines that mixes arg parsing, bignum allocation, addition and printing. The hand-rolled bignum is far more machinery than the task needs. There is no dead code or debug output.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The `calloc` results are never NULL-checked. C uses `strtol(argv[1], NULL, 10)` without checking endptr, so "abc" prints 0 with exit 0. `if (argc < 2) return 1;` exits silently with no usage message. Python has no argc check (it raises IndexError). Negative input prints 0 in both languages.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: f(0), f(1) and large n are correct and iterative in both languages, and bignum exceeds 93 (the n=500 outputs match). But bad arguments are not cleanly rejected: in C, non-numeric or negative input prints 0 with exit 0; Python prints 0 for negatives, and a missing argument gives a raw IndexError traceback.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: Compiles with plain gcc; the log shows no warnings even under `-Wall -Wextra -pedantic`. `python3 -W error` ran cleanly. Each mode prints only the number. No extra flags or environment variables are needed.
